reference.source: Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology / Cornea by Krachmer
clinicalPearls: A slowly progressive, usually painless, bilateral but often asymmetric peripheral corneal thinning, classically beginning superiorly
The epithelium remains intact over the thinned gutter, distinguishing it from ulcerative processes such as Mooren ulcer
A fine yellow-white lipid deposit is often seen at the advancing central edge of the thinning
Superficial vascularisation (pannus) crosses into the area of thinning as the degeneration progresses
Progressive thinning induces marked against-the-rule or oblique astigmatism, which is often the main cause of reduced vision
Typically affects middle-aged adults and is generally non-inflammatory, though an uncommon inflammatory variant with episodic redness and pain exists
Management is largely optical (spectacles or contact lenses for astigmatism), reserving lamellar keratoplasty or tectonic grafting for severe thinning or perforation risk
Spontaneous or minor-trauma perforation can occur in advanced disease because of the marked thinning
reference.pathophysiology: Terrien marginal degeneration is a non-inflammatory (in its usual form) peripheral corneal thinning of uncertain cause, in which the peripheral stroma progressively degenerates and thins while the overlying epithelium stays intact. Lipid is deposited at the leading edge and superficial vessels grow into the gutter. The thinning typically starts superiorly and gradually extends circumferentially, producing a shallow peripheral trough. Progressive structural weakening flattens the peripheral cornea and steepens the meridian at right angles, generating high against-the-rule or oblique astigmatism, and severe thinning predisposes to perforation.
additionalDifferentials: Mooren ulcer and other peripheral ulcerative keratitis
Peripheral ulcerative keratitis from systemic vasculitis
Marginal furrow degeneration in the elderly
Dellen (localised thinning from adjacent surface elevation)
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination documenting peripheral thinning with intact epithelium and a lipid line
Corneal topography to characterise the induced astigmatism
Anterior segment optical coherence tomography or pachymetry to quantify thinning
Inflammatory and autoimmune workup to exclude peripheral ulcerative keratitis when signs are atypical
Refraction to assess the visual impact of astigmatism
redFlags: Severe thinning with risk of spontaneous or traumatic perforation
New pain and redness suggesting the uncommon inflammatory variant or an alternative diagnosis
Rapid progression atypical for this usually indolent degeneration
Epithelial breakdown raising concern for an ulcerative or infective process
reference.prognosis: The degeneration is usually slowly progressive with vision limited mainly by astigmatism, which can often be managed optically. Advanced thinning carries a risk of perforation and may require tectonic surgery, but the condition rarely leads to central corneal opacification.
pitfalls: Confusing painless thinning with the painful ulceration of Mooren ulcer
Missing high against-the-rule astigmatism as the true cause of reduced vision
Underestimating perforation risk in advanced thinning
Failing to recognise the rarer inflammatory variant
references: Cornea by Krachmer, Mannis and Holland
